image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic #447: Too Old For This Shit

titleText.es: Dicen que si un matemático no ha publicado su gran obra a la edad de 11 años, nunca lo hará.
titleText.en: They say if a mathematician doesn't do their great work by age eleven, they never will.
titleText.noteEn: The title text extends the joke by moving the supposed deadline for a mathematician's major work down to age eleven. The Spanish archive phrases the achievement specifically as publishing the great work and prints 11 as digits.

regions.labelEs: ME GUSTARÍA PODER DARLE A LAS MATEMÁTICAS COMO CUANDO ERA JOVEN.

applications.explanationEn: Me identifies the person with the wish, gustaría makes the request conditional and polite, and poder stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the desired action.
Gustaría keeps the whole dictionary form gustar and adds the conditional ending -ía.
Poder expresses ability, and dar remains in its unchanged dictionary form inside darle.
The following a las matemáticas selects the activity sense of darle rather than a literal act of giving.
Darle supplies the colloquial activity verb, a introduces the activity, and las matemáticas fills that activity slot.
Era uses the imperfect because it presents being young as a background state in the past rather than one bounded event.

regions.labelEs: NO ME RESULTA TAN FÁCIL COMO ANTES.

applications.explanationEn: Me identifies the person experiencing the judgment, and fácil supplies that judgment, so resulta has its seems-or-is-found sense here.
Me marks the speaker as the person with the judgment, resulta matches the singular thing being judged, and fácil supplies the description; tan only adjusts its degree.
Tan introduces the degree of fácil, and como opens the comparison.

regions.labelEs: LA MATEMÁTICA ES UN JUEGO PARA LOS JÓVENES. TENGO QUE ECHARME A UN LADO Y DAR PASO AL FUTURO.

applications.explanationEn: Tengo matches the speaker, que completes the obligation pattern, and echar stays in its unchanged dictionary form inside echarme.
Me is attached directly to the unchanged verb echar, making the one-word form echarme.
The following fixed words a un lado select the step-aside sense of echarme.
Echarme supplies the speaker's form of echarse, and a un lado completes the fixed expression.
The following paso al futuro selects the make-way sense of dar rather than literal giving.
Dar paso supplies the change expression, al combines a with el, and futuro fills the slot for what follows.
Tienes matches the addressed person, trece supplies the age number, and años names the years used in the Spanish age pattern.

regions.labelEs: SÍ, Y YA ES HORA DE QUE LO ACEPTE.

applications.exampleEs: ES HORA DE QUE LO ACEPTE
applications.explanationEn: Es hora de que introduces an action that is now due, and acepte is the special form of aceptar used for that pending action; lo is the visible object inside the action but not part of the trigger.
Lo replaces the thing being accepted and stands directly before the changed verb acepte.

cards.answerEn: marks me as the person who likes something
cards.noteEn: With gustar, Spanish presents the liked thing as pleasing to a person. Me identifies the speaker as that person; it does not become a separate English word when the natural translation uses “I.”

cards.questionEn: How do you politely say that someone would like to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person, then gustaría, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The short word identifies who has the wish: me gustaría means “I would like,” te gustaría means “you would like,” os gustaría means “you all would like” in Spain, and le gustaría can mean “he, she, or formal you would like.” Gustaría stays singular because the following activity is treated as the thing that would be pleasing.

example.en: I would like to learn Italian.

cards.answerEn: would like; would be pleasing
cards.noteEn: Gustaría is gustar with the ending -ía. With a short word such as me, te, or le, it politely says who would like something: me gustaría means “I would like.”

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

cards.answerEn: to be able to; can

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: to do; to be into an activity (with a)
cards.noteEn: In the colloquial pattern darle a una actividad, darle means to do that activity, practice it, or spend time on it. The attached le is part of the expression rather than a separately named recipient.

cards.questionEn: How do you colloquially say that someone does, practices, or is into an activity?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of darle, then a, then name the activity.
cards.noteEn: In this informal pattern, dar changes for the person and time, while the attached le and the following a remain. The activity may include a small word such as el or la: darle al ajedrez, darle a la fotografía. This expression is common in conversation but is less neutral than simply naming the activity with hacer, practicar, or jugar.

example.es: Mis amigos le dan al ciclismo.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links darle to an activity
cards.noteEn: This a is required in the colloquial pattern darle a una actividad. It introduces the activity that someone does or practices.

cards.answerEn: the (feminine plural)
mathematics; math
like; as (making a comparison)
cards.noteEn: Unaccented como can introduce the person, thing, or situation used for a comparison. It does not ask “how”; the question word cómo has an accent.

cards.answerEn: when
was; used to be
cards.noteEn: Era is a past form of ser used for a background state, description, or ongoing past situation. This form is called the imperfect.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.answerEn: young
huh?; what?
cards.noteEn: Eh can show that the speaker is surprised or did not understand what was just said.

cards.answerEn: no; not
to me; marks me as the person who finds something a certain way
cards.noteEn: With resultar plus a description, me identifies the speaker as the person experiencing that judgment. Natural English often makes that person the subject: me resulta difícil is commonly expressed as “I find it difficult.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone finds something easy, difficult, strange, or similar?
cards.answerEn: Name the thing, add me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person, then use a form of resultar and a describing word.
cards.noteEn: The thing being judged controls the form of resultar: la tarea me resulta fácil, las tareas me resultan fáciles. The short word before resultar identifies the person who experiences the judgment. English often makes that person the subject and says “I find...” or “it seems... to me.” An adjective is a word such as fácil or extraño that describes the thing.

cards.answerEn: seems; feels; is found to be (by someone)
cards.noteEn: Resulta is a present form of resultar for one thing. With me, te, le, nos, os, or les and a description, it says how that thing seems or feels to a person.

cards.answerEn: as (before a description in tan… como)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that two things are equally strong in some quality?
cards.answerEn: Put tan before the describing word and como before the comparison: tan… como means “as… as.”
cards.noteEn: A describing word can describe a thing, such as claro (“clear”), or how an action happens, such as rápido (“quickly”). Tan and como stay unchanged; only the surrounding words change as the surrounding grammar requires.

example.es: El café está tan frío como el agua.
example.en: The coffee is as cold as the water.

cards.answerEn: easy
cards.noteEn: The opposite is difícil, ‘difficult.’ Fácil keeps its written accent in the singular.

cards.answerEn: before; earlier; in the past
cards.noteEn: Used by itself, antes can point back to an earlier time rather than introducing a following event.

cards.answerEn: uh-huh; I see
cards.noteEn: Ajá is a short acknowledgment showing that someone is following or has understood what was said. Tone can also make it skeptical.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; Spanish uses la before a general abstract idea such as vida
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses el or la when discussing an idea in general, while English uses the bare noun without “the.” The article still matches the noun: la vida, la paciencia, el tiempo.

cards.answerEn: mathematics; math
cards.noteEn: The singular matemática can name mathematics as a field. The plural matemáticas is also very common for the subject or activity.

cards.answerEn: is; belongs to the stated category
cards.noteEn: Es is the present form of ser used for one person or thing. Between two naming words, it identifies or classifies the first as the second.

cards.answerEn: a; an (masculine)
game
for; introduces what something is suitable for
cards.noteEn: After adecuado or a matching form such as adecuada or adecuados, para introduces the intended use, person, situation, or action.

example.es: Esta mesa es adecuada para niños.
example.en: This table is suitable for children.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; Spanish uses the article before a general group
cards.noteEn: Spanish normally uses los before a plural group discussed as a whole, as in los programadores. English often leaves “the” out and simply says “programmers” when making the same general statement.

cards.answerEn: young people
cards.noteEn: A describing word such as joven can stand for people when the person-word is understood. Los jóvenes means young people as a group.

example.en: The young people organized the event.

cards.answerEn: I have

cards.promptEs: tener que + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tener, then que, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only tener changes for the person and time: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, and so on. The final action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes tener que, “to have to”
to step aside; to move myself out of the way (with a un lado)
cards.noteEn: Echarme combines the unchanged verb echar with me. In echarme a un lado, the full expression means that the speaker steps aside or gets out of the way.

example.es: Voy a echarme a un lado.
example.en: I am going to step aside.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone steps aside or gets out of the way?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of echarse followed by a un lado.
cards.noteEn: Echar changes for the person and time, and the attached short word changes with the person: me echo, te echas, se echa, nos echamos. A un lado stays fixed. The expression can describe a physical move or, figuratively, letting someone or something else take over.

example.es: Nos echamos a un lado para dejarlos pasar.
example.en: We stepped aside to let them pass.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of echarse a un lado
cards.noteEn: This a is the fixed link between echarse and un lado in the expression for stepping aside.

cards.answerEn: side
and
to give way; to make way (with paso a)
cards.noteEn: Dar normally means to give. In dar paso a, it forms the conventional expression for allowing someone or something to follow or replace what came before.

example.es: La lluvia da paso al sol.
example.en: The rain gives way to sunshine.

cards.promptEs: dar paso a + persona o cosa
cards.questionEn: How do you say that one thing gives way to or makes way for another?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of dar, then paso a, then name what follows or replaces it.
cards.noteEn: Only dar changes for the person and time; paso a stays together. Before el, a and el combine as al: dar paso al invierno. The expression can describe a literal passage or a change in which something new follows.

example.es: El invierno da paso a la primavera.

cards.answerEn: way; passage (as part of dar paso a)
cards.noteEn: Paso can mean a step or passage. Together with dar and a, it forms dar paso a, “to give way to” or “to make way for.”

example.es: La noche da paso al día.

cards.answerEn: to the (a + el)
cards.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

cards.answerEn: future
you are (stating age); literally, you have
cards.noteEn: Spanish states age with tener, “to have.” Tienes is the present form for one person addressed informally, so tienes trece años means that the listener is thirteen years old.

cards.questionEn: How do you state someone's age in years?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of tener, then the number, then años.
cards.noteEn: Spanish describes age as years that a person “has,” so tener changes to match the person: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen. English instead uses “to be.” Año becomes singular only for exactly one year: tiene un año.

cards.answerEn: thirteen
years
cards.noteEn: Años is the plural of año. Keep the ñ: anos without it is a different word.

example.en: We lived there for two years.

cards.answerEn: yes
now; by now
it is (in an impersonal time expression)
cards.noteEn: Spanish can use es without a separate subject word in expressions such as es hora, “it is time.” English supplies the impersonal word “it.”

cards.promptEs: es hora de que + acción pendiente
cards.questionEn: How do you say that it is time for someone to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use es hora de que, then put the action in the special form used for something that should now happen.
cards.noteEn: Es hora de que introduces an action as due or called for, not as a reported fact. Spanish therefore uses a special verb form called the subjunctive. For a regular -ar verb, the ordinary ending switches to e: trabaja becomes trabaje and acepta becomes acepte. The action verb still changes to match the person who should act. When no separate doer needs to be named, Spanish can instead use es hora de plus the unchanged dictionary form: es hora de salir.

example.es: Es hora de que Marta trabaje.
example.en: It is time for Marta to work.

cards.answerEn: time; the moment to act
cards.noteEn: After es, hora can identify the appropriate moment for an action rather than a clock hour.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of es hora de que
cards.noteEn: De is the required link between hora and que when the following group of words has its own action and names who should act.

example.es: Es hora de que Marta vuelva.
example.en: It is time for Marta to return.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes es hora de que before the action
cards.noteEn: Que completes the time-to-act expression before a group of words with its own action. The following verb uses a special form because the action is called for rather than reported as a fact.

example.es: Es hora de que Marta vuelva.
example.en: It is time for Marta to return.

cards.answerEn: it (direct-object pronoun)
cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

cards.answerEn: I accept (special form for an action that is called for)
cards.noteEn: Acepte is a form of aceptar used after a trigger such as es hora de que. The ordinary statement form for the speaker, acepto, changes to acepte because the acceptance is being urged or treated as pending, not stated as a fact. The same written form can also match he, she, or formal you; context identifies the speaker here.

example.es: Es hora de que yo acepte el resultado.
example.en: It is time for me to accept the result.
